The boy peeks furtively from the volume of his mother's skirts, scrubbing at his tears with tiny fists clad in black cotton gloves. 

"Maman, I cannot bear to see him!" 

"Hush, my little chick– Monsieur, my apologies for my son… he has never…" 

"Beheld the beloved dead," the man from the pulpit says, matter-of-fact, and nods, "If I may…?" 

With a small gesture of her hand, the mother consents, and gently separates from the boy, who stands brave and puffy-eyed before the tall man, eyes screwed to the floor as he sniffles. The man, with apparent difficulty, lowers himself to kneel on one knee– you can see the primal expression of pain pinching his features even from your vantage point– and talks to the boy, soft and low and lulling, so low that you cannot hear as the two speak and the man gently clasps the boy's hands. 

There has been a stony cast to the man's demeanor until this moment, when he softens a mote imperceptibly, and you silently slip nearer, choosing a shadowy alcove in which to ensconce yourself to view the tableau better, a story unfolding before your eyes. 

"It is good, I think, to say goodbye to those you love. And your love held him dearest in your heart, I take it?" The man asks the boy.
- The boy nods wordlessly, sniffling, scrubbing at his eyes again. They are the color of cerulean; oft considered a mark of luck in Ishgard, to have such a shade of blue in the eyes. Azure. Fortuitous portent found in this boy who struggles to confront the finality of death. You hang your head, watching them through your lashes. 

"In my work," The man says softly, taking the boy gently by the shoulders, "I could hardly gainsay I have loved him as gently as you; I have bathed him, shaved his face carefully, dressed him meticulously to ready him for this goodbye. There is naught to fear in the company of the departed; naught else but the enormity of one's own grief. Your mother tells me it is your ambition to become a Knight Dragoon, is that correct?"

The boy, face reddened, nods profusely and stammers a "Yes," little fists clenched at his sides, in the woolen fabric of his little black hose. 

"Allow yourself this first victory over Death, beloved," The man says, "And I will be as your seneschal." 

He extends his hand, and the child after some small hesitation takes it. They walk together to the casket, hand in hand.
- As you approach, his closest approximation to a welcoming expression goes cold as a snuffed candle and finally the other half of his lopsided mouth evens into one irascible pinch, and though his eyes are unmoving and focused on the procession of mourners filtering out of St. Reymanaud's, he does have the good grace to address you, "What is it you need..." 

"No way to address the grieved, Ser," you say. For all his poise and the unflinching patience he'd shown that toddling child not even a bell ago (even if still a bit terse), he is rude, as if your presence is no more than an intrusion on a strictly regimented plan. Your next word would blow a house of cards down, and he is cross for it. 

Gaze still pinned on the crowd, he squints a little, minute lines at the corners of his eyes betray an exhaustion surely beyond his years, and he leans toward you casually, his fougere of deepwood fern, resinous, spicy and slightly acrid wafts into your nose, your mouth, "You lie," his caustic tone belies his placid expression and he gives a wave and a nod at a departing mourner who gives him a sad smile and leaves, sniffling into her handkerchief, "You are not of the grieved. 4. Mix together cream cheese and sugar. Set to one side.

6. Cut out rounds with a 3 inch pastry cutter and line greased mince pie tins with these disks.
7. Fill to half depth with mincemeat and then top with a teaspoonful of cream cheese mixture -
- 8. Roll out the remaining pastry and cut out tops with a 2-inch cutter. Moisten the edges with water and place on top of filled bases, pressing lightly to seal.
9. Brush tops with milk and bake for 15-20 minutes until lightly golden.
10. As the pastry is so crumbly, allow these to cool in the tin before very gently easing from the tin with a rounded knife.
11. Serve warmed in the oven and sprinkled with icing sugar.
